## Welcome {#home}

### Blindness and Visual Impairment

**Learning Objectives:**

- Define blindness using WHO's visual acuity criteria
- Identify the leading causes of blindness in India
- Describe cataract as the single largest treatable cause
- Outline India's NPCBVI strategy and school eye-screening programmes

🟢 **MUST KNOW** · 🟡 **SHOULD KNOW** · 🟣 **MAY KNOW** · 🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.notes}
Blindness prevention connects back to trachoma (already named in the
"Other Infections" module as a preventable infectious cause) and to
diabetes (diabetic retinopathy, Module 1) — this module gives blindness
its own dedicated epidemiological treatment as its own major NCD-linked
public health problem.
:::

---

## Defining and Measuring Blindness {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

**WHO definition of blindness:** visual acuity of **less than 3/60** in
the better eye with best possible correction (i.e. even with glasses,
unable to see at 3 metres what a person with normal vision sees at 60
metres).

- **Low vision** — visual acuity between 3/60 and 6/18 in the better
  eye — impaired but not meeting the blindness threshold
- India periodically conducts **National Blindness and Visual
  Impairment Surveys** to track prevalence and the changing distribution
  of causes over time — the same registry/survey logic already seen for
  cancer (previous module) applied here

---

## Leading Causes of Blindness in India {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

- **Cataract** — by far the **single largest cause** of blindness in
  India, and critically, a **treatable/reversible** cause via surgery —
  making it the top priority target for blindness-control programmes
- **Refractive error** — uncorrected, a major cause of avoidable visual
  impairment, especially in children, correctable simply with glasses
- **Corneal blindness** — from infection, injury, or vitamin A
  deficiency (recall Chapter 9's nutrition content)
- **Glaucoma** — progressive optic nerve damage, often asymptomatic
  until advanced, making screening important since damage already done
  cannot be reversed
- **Diabetic retinopathy** — a direct link to Module 1's diabetes
  complications content; increasingly significant as India's diabetes
  burden grows

**Exam pattern:** cataract's dominance, combined with its
treatability, is *why* India's blindness-control strategy centres so
heavily on cataract surgical coverage.

---

## NPCBVI: India's National Programme {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

The **National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual
Impairment (NPCBVI)** — renamed and expanded from the original National
Programme for Control of Blindness to explicitly include visual
impairment, not only blindness — pursues:

- **Cataract surgical services** — the programme's largest single
  activity, given cataract's dominant, treatable share of the burden
- **School eye-screening programmes** — identifying uncorrected
  refractive error in children early, since undetected poor vision
  directly affects learning — connecting blindness control to the
  Under-Five Clinic and school health content (Chapter 14)
- **Integration with the general health system** — following the same
  primary-care integration logic already seen for leprosy (NLEP) and
  mental health (DMHP) — vision screening delivered through existing
  health infrastructure rather than a separate parallel system

## Self-Check: Question 1 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 1

WHO defines blindness as visual acuity, with best correction, of:

- Less than 6/18
- [Less than 3/60]{.correct data-explanation="WHO defines blindness as visual acuity less than 3/60 in the better eye with best possible correction; 3/60 to 6/18 defines low vision instead."}
- Less than 6/6
- Any uncorrected refractive error
:::
